title: Generative sampling with physics-informed kernels
comment: Proceedings of 42nd International Symposium on Lattice Field Theory (LATTICE2025), November 2-8 2025, TIFR, Mumbai, India
summary: We construct a generative network for Monte-Carlo sampling in lattice field theories and beyond, for which the layerwise propagation is computed and optimised independently on each layer. The architecture uses physics-informed renormalisation group flows that provide access to the layerwise propagation step from one layer to the next in terms of a simple first order partial differential equation for the respective renormalisation group kernel through a given layer. Thus, it transforms the generative task into that of solving once the set of independent and linear differential equations for the kernels of the transformation. As these equations are analytically known, the kernels can be refined iteratively. This allows us to structurally tackle out-of-domain problems generally encountered in generative models and opens the path to further optimisation. We illustrate the practical feasibility of the architecture within simulations in scalar field theories.

AI.tldr: A novel generative network for Monte-Carlo sampling in lattice field theories, using physics-informed renormalisation group flows to solve linear differential equations for transformation kernels, enabling iterative refinement and addressing out-of-domain problems. Demonstrated through simulations in scalar field theories.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop a more efficient and structurally sound approach to Monte-Carlo sampling within the context of lattice field theories. The authors aim to address common issues with generative models, particularly those related to out-of-domain problems, by leveraging known physical principles to inform the design of the network architecture.
AI.method: The method involves creating a generative network where each layer's propagation is computed independently, utilizing physics-informed renormalisation group flows. These flows allow the calculation of the transformation from one layer to the next as a solution to a first-order partial differential equation for the corresponding kernel. This process transforms the problem into solving a set of independent and linear differential equations, which can then be iteratively refined.
AI.result: The result is a new framework for generative modeling that is capable of handling out-of-domain issues by iteratively improving the kernels used for transformations between layers. The feasibility of this approach is demonstrated through its application in simulations of scalar field theories, suggesting potential for broader applications in lattice field theories and beyond.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion drawn is that the proposed generational network, by employing physics-informed renormalisation group flows, provides an effective and flexible method for Monte-Carlo sampling. It not only overcomes limitations associated with traditional generative models but also opens up opportunities for further optimization and extension to other areas of theoretical physics.

title: Meson spectroscopy from lattice QCD
comment: Proceedings of a plenary talk at the MESON conference (Kraków, June 2026)
summary: Determining the meson spectrum directly from Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) remains a central challenge, since QCD is strongly coupled at low energies and most excited states appear as resonances in hadronic decay channels. Advances in lattice QCD and scattering theory now provide a systematic framework for extracting meson spectra and resonance properties from first principles. Here I present an overview of this program and review current state-of-the-art calculations in meson spectroscopy from lattice QCD. I highlight recent progress in the extraction of resonant and coupled-channel amplitudes, along with frontier developments in three-body dynamics and the determination of meson photo-couplings. Together, these advances are bringing us closer to a comprehensive first-principles description of the excited meson spectrum.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the latest advances in meson spectroscopy using lattice QCD, focusing on the extraction of resonant and coupled-channel amplitudes, three-body dynamics, and meson photo-couplings, to provide a comprehensive first-principles description of the excited meson spectrum.
AI.motivation: The motivation of this paper is to address the central challenge of determining the meson spectrum directly from Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), especially at low energies where QCD is strongly coupled, and most excited states appear as resonances in hadronic decay channels. The aim is to leverage recent developments in lattice QCD and scattering theory for a more accurate and systematic approach to extracting meson spectra and resonance properties.
AI.method: The method involves employing lattice QCD simulations combined with advanced techniques in scattering theory to systematically extract meson spectra and their properties. This includes the analysis of resonant and coupled-channel amplitudes, exploration of three-body dynamics, and the determination of meson photo-couplings, all grounded in first principles calculations.
AI.result: The results indicate significant progress in the field of meson spectroscopy, with state-of-the-art calculations now capable of accurately describing not only the basic properties of mesons but also more complex phenomena such as three-body interactions and meson photo-couplings. These advancements are contributing to a more complete understanding of the excited meson spectrum based on fundamental principles.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion drawn from this work is that by integrating cutting-edge computational methods with theoretical physics, we are making substantial strides towards achieving a comprehensive and detailed first-principles description of the excited meson spectrum. The ongoing research promises to further our understanding of QCD and its implications for particle physics.
